# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Collections of time series can often be aggregated at several levels by geography, product, or other attributes.
Forecasts are usually needed for every series at every level, and they should be coherent: each aggregate forecast should equal the sum of the forecasts below it.
Forecast reconciliation achieves this by forecasting every series independently and then adjusting the forecasts to satisfy the aggregation constraints [@hyndman2011optimal; @athanasopoulos2023forecast].
The minimum trace (MinT) method of @wickramasuriya2019optimal chooses the adjustment using the covariance matrix of the base forecast errors, and it is now the standard approach.

Reconciliation is almost always applied to one variable at a time, yet many hierarchies carry several variables.
A retailer, for example, may need forecasts of both unit sales and revenue for every store, with each variable summing across stores to regional and national totals.
The two variables are measured in different units, but both respond to the same promotions, holidays and local demand, so their forecast errors are correlated.
Because MinT works by exploiting the covariance of the base forecast errors, it seems natural to reconcile both variables together, using a covariance matrix that spans them, and to expect this to beat reconciling each separately.
This paper explores when joint reconciliation is better than reconciling each variable separately.

Joint reconciliation of several variables is not the same problem as reconciling a grouped hierarchy.
In a grouped hierarchy, such as sales disaggregated by both region and product type, the categories of each grouping variable are linked by aggregation constraints: total sales is the sum over products or over regions, and that total is itself forecast.
Here unit sales are never added to revenue.
The stacked summing matrix is block diagonal by variable, and the only link between the variables is the error covariance.

To address this question, we consider MinT as a regression of the base forecast errors on the observed incoherences of the base forecasts.
Joint reconciliation of several variables coincides with separate reconciliation if and only if, once each variable has been reconciled on its own, its remaining errors are uncorrelated with the incoherences of every other variable.
Two known results are special cases.
MinT is unaffected by any component of the error covariance that lies in the coherent subspace [@wickramasuriya2021properties], so cross-variable dependence of that form is invisible.
When the error covariance is separable, a Kronecker product of a cross-variable matrix and a cross-series matrix, joint and separate reconciliation coincide whatever the cross-variable correlation.
This is a special case of a result of @girolimetto2025cross for cross-temporal reconciliation, and the reconciliation analogue of Zellner's observation [@zellner1962efficient] that seemingly unrelated regressions with identical regressors reduce to equation-by-equation least squares.

In practice, we need to know whether each variable's separately reconciled errors are correlated with the other variables' incoherences, and if so, how much this affects the forecasts.
We propose two effect sizes: $\kappa$, the weight that the joint reconciliation places on other variables' incoherences, and $\gamma$, the reduction in mean squared error that it would deliver if the estimated covariance were correct.
We also propose a likelihood ratio test of the characterising condition, which uses the regression form of MinT and needs no simulation.

Two experiments show how little joint reconciliation offers.
When the error covariance is known, even substantial departures from separability reduce the mean squared error by at most `r num$gainFtwoBrazilMax`% in our designs, and usually by much less.
When it is estimated, joint reconciliation pays for the extra cross-variable blocks: with separable errors it is worse than separate reconciliation at small sample sizes, and it recovers small population gains only with long series.
With fitted ARIMA and VAR base models, joint and separate reconciliation are indistinguishable for series of typical monthly length.
In an application to monthly worker admissions and dismissals in Brazil's 27 federative units, which aggregate to five regions and to the country, the test detects a small correlation between each variable's separately reconciled errors and the other variable's incoherences, but with ARIMA base forecasts joint reconciliation does not systematically improve the forecasts of either admissions or dismissals.

Joint modelling does matter for quantities that combine the variables.
Net employment change, the difference between admissions and dismissals, is the headline figure in Brazil's official monthly employment statistics.
MinT with the true covariance is optimal in the positive semidefinite order, so when such correlation is present, joint reconciliation can help a combination of variables even when it does not help any variable on its own.
In the application it reduces the mean squared error of the national net change by `r num$appNetPointTotal`%.
For probabilistic forecasts, most of the gain comes before reconciliation: simulating the base forecasts jointly, so that the dependence between the variables is kept, reduces the CRPS of the national net change by `r num$appNetJointSepTotal`%, and reconciling the paths jointly raises this to `r num$appNetJointJointTotal`%.
